To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the functional connectome derived using simultaneously acquired EEG and fMRI data can provide a more accurate and complete description of the functional connectivity of the brain than can either modality alone.

(1) EEG-fMRI connectivity can be used to probe the functional connectivity in the human brain, (2) the EEG-fMRI connectivity is sensitive to the state of the brain, (3) the EEG-fMR connectivity is sensitive to brain pathology, and (4) the EEG-fM connectivity is sensitive to genetic factors.
simultaneous EEG-fMRI can be used to: 1) identify functional networks in the human brain, and 2) identify the spatial and temporal dynamics of functional networks in the brain.

the following questions: (i) How does the functional connectivity derived from simultaneous EEG and fMRI relate to that derived from each modality alone?

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there are still many open questions regarding the relationship between EEG and fMRI, which is a topic of active current research.

the EEG and fMRI functional connectomes are complementary, with EEG being sensitive to fast, low-level, local processes while fMRI is sensitive to slower, higher-level, more widespread activity (Jorge et al., 14).
EEG and fMRI are two different measures, with different sensitivity and temporal resolution.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the EEG and fMRI connectomes are complementary and can be combined to provide a richer picture of brain connectivity.
we have shown how to combine the complementary strengths of fMRI and EEG to provide a more robust estimate of functional brain connectivity, and that this can be used for a range of applications.
we are able to construct a functional brain connectome from EEG, which is then used to inform a functional connectome constructed from fMRI.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the combination of EEG and fMRI data can lead to a more comprehensive understanding of brain function.
EEG can be used to provide a complementary perspective to fMRI, and the two modalities can be used to probe different aspects of brain activity.
the EEG and MRI measures can be combined to provide a more complete description of brain activity.
